<div class="hmi-analyte-explorer" id="hmi-occurrence-dried-herbs" data-analyte-explorer data-compact-intro="true" data-source-summaries="true"><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure" data-explorer-context><summary data-open-context aria-haspopup="dialog" aria-controls="hmi-occurrence-dried-herbs-drawer">Comparison methods and scope</summary><div data-explorer-context-content>

<p>Each row is one statistic a source reports for one form of dried herbs, group and metal; percentiles, ranges and maxima reported for the same samples as a mean or median are shown on that row. Different forms and preparation states are kept apart, and dry-weight results never share a reference with as-sold or fresh-weight results. Ratings place a result against an HMI reference built from monitoring results and ordinary-setting medians for the same form and basis. Same-study contrasts compare a contaminated or treated site with its control, targeted with random sampling, a prepared form with the unprocessed one, or one group of a study with the median of its other groups. Held rows failed a check against their own source and are shown but not compared.</p>

data-shared-occurrence-methods><summary>Shared dataset methods and interpretation</summary><div data-shared-evidence-content><p>Source summaries retain their original statistic, material, basis and censoring. Each source drawer identifies methods and overlapping samples. No matched reference or pooled distribution is inferred.</p></div></details><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure" data-baseline-fallback id="hmi-reference-hmi-pooled-reference-v2:dried-herbs-5438245227d6:b2ae13ab78a5"><summary>HMI dried herbs Pb reference · Dried Herbs, as sold</summary><div data-baseline-reference-template="hmi-pooled-reference-v2:dried-herbs-5438245227d6:b2ae13ab78a5"><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Reference and scope</p><p>HMI dried herbs Pb reference · Dried Herbs, as sold. Dried Herbs, as sold; As sold, as eaten or fresh weight, µg/kg; no moisture conversion. Distribution of subgroup median concentration values.</p><div class="hmi-drawer-table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Reference (µg/kg)</th><th scope="col">Q1</th><th scope="col">Median</th><th scope="col">Q3</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Primary HMI reference</td><td>295–300 (bounded)</td><td>2600</td><td>2600</td></tr><tr><td>Alternative weighting</td><td>290–300 (bounded)</td><td>2600</td><td>2600</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p>73 reference units; 2 sampling families. Counts describe evidence units, not independent studies or certainty.</p><div class="hmi-drawer-table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Contributing family</th><th scope="col">Reference units</th><th scope="col">Weight</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>WHO GEMS/Food</td><td>72</td><td>50%</td></tr><tr><td>Angelon-Gaetz et al. 2018</td><td>1</td><td>50%</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Methods</p><p>HMI pools subgroup medians for dried herbs, as sold on a as sold, as eaten or fresh weight basis: monitoring results summarized as one median per reporting region, sampling type and collection year, total diet composites and printed sample values as single observations, and printed subgroup medians from ordinary farms or markets. Each sampling family has equal total weight. Non-detects stay as zero-to-limit intervals, so quartiles carry lower and upper bounds. Means, ranges and maxima never enter as observations. Other forms, other bases, targeted sampling and results from mining, industrial, wastewater-affected, experimental, fertiliser or manufacturer settings are kept out of this reference.</p><p>Inverse weighted empirical CDF; midpoint at exact cumulative-weight boundaries. At least four reference units and a definitely positive Q1 to Q3 spread are required. This is a display eligibility rule, not statistical validation.</p><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Limitations</p><p>2 sampling families with different designs; none is a probability sample of world supply. Reporting regions and purchase markets are not growing areas. Non-detects with differing limits widen the bounds. A position is descriptive concentration, not a safety or compliance judgment.</p><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Admitted source families</p><ul><li><a href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants" class="internal" data-slug="sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants" data-no-cite-meta>WHO GEMS/Food</a></li><li><a href="../sources/angelon-gaetz2018-lead-spices-north-carolina" class="internal" data-slug="sources/angelon-gaetz2018-lead-spices-north-carolina" data-no-cite-meta>Angelon-Gaetz et al. 2018</a></li></ul><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure"><summary>Reference version and interpretation</summary><p>Frozen evidence selection: 2026-10-22. Method: hmi-pooled-reference-v2.</p><p>hmi-pooled-reference-v2:dried-herbs-5438245227d6:b2ae13ab78a5</p><p>The reference is computed by HMI from admitted evidence, not copied from a study baseline. Results depend on the method and its reporting limit. Reporting limits for lead ranged from 1 µg/kg (WHO GEMS/Food) to 4,000 µg/kg (WHO GEMS/Food), so a non-detect from a less sensitive method says much less.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Reporting limits for cadmium ranged from 0.4 µg/kg (WHO GEMS/Food) to 200 µg/kg (WHO GEMS/Food), so a non-detect from a less sensitive method says much less.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Reporting limits for total arsenic ranged from 10 µg/kg (WHO GEMS/Food) to 1,020 µg/kg (WHO GEMS/Food), so a non-detect from a less sensitive method says much less.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

A useful lot result names the form, the basis and a quantification limit well below the limit that applies.

Every source record that names dried Herbs was decided on its content: 18 occurrence extracted, 18 records in all. The occurrence table renders every extracted result; held values remain visible with their reason.

References identify the sources used in these answers. The Sources index preserves additional discovery links; inclusion there does not mean a source has been reviewed for this assessment. Corrections, completed searches, new direct evidence and changes in requirements should reopen the relevant answer.


<a id="universal-faqs"></a>
## Dried Herbs FAQs

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="what-heavy-metals-are-found-in-dried-herbs" data-anchor="what-heavy-metals-are-found-in-dried-herbs" data-question="What heavy metals are found in dried Herbs?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>What heavy metals are found in dried Herbs?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

The library reports lead, cadmium, total arsenic, inorganic arsenic, dimethylarsinic acid, total mercury, nickel, chromium, aluminium, tin, Co, Cu, Fe, Mn and Zn in dried Herbs, most often lead, cadmium and total arsenic.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/angelon-gaetz2018-lead-spices-north-carolina|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Angelon-Gaetz KA, Klaus C, Chaudhry EA, Bean DK · 2018</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/angelon-gaetz2018-lead-spices-north-carolina">Lead in Spices, Herbal Remedies, and Ceremonial Powders Sampled from Home Investigations for Children with Elevated Blood Lead Levels — North Carolina, 2011–2018</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">MMWR Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/angelon-gaetz2018-lead-spices-north-carolina">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/mustatea2021-romania-food-supplements-lead-cadmium|3]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Mustatea G, Ungureanu EL, Iorga SC, Ciotea D, Popa ME · 2021</span><a class="cite-card-title" →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/kowalska2021-metals-herbs-spices-tea-coffee-poland|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Kowalska G · 2021</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/kowalska2021-metals-herbs-spices-tea-coffee-poland">The Safety Assessment of Toxic Metals in Commonly Used Herbs, Spices, Tea, and Coffee in <details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="which-types-of-dried-herbs-have-the-lowest-levels" data-anchor="which-types-of-dried-herbs-have-the-lowest-levels" data-question="Which types of dried Herbs have the lowest levels?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Which types of dried Herbs have the lowest levels?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

For lead, the HMI reference median was lowest for dried Herbs, as sold (200 µg/kg) and highest for dried Herbs, dried (3,860 µg/kg); forms differ in water content, so this compares foods as sold or eaten, not uptake.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/authors2025-instrumentation-for-monitoring-toxic-elements-in-food-matrices|8]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span href="../sources/authors2025-instrumentation-for-monitoring-toxic-elements-in-food-matrices">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/winiarska-mieczan2023-cd-pb-polish-herbs-spices|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Winiarska-Mieczan A, Jachimowicz K, Kwiecień M, Krusiński R, Kislova S, Sowińska L, Zasadna Z, Yanovych D · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/winiarska-mieczan2023-cd-pb-polish-herbs-spices">The Content of Cd and Pb </div>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="which-regions-report-the-lowest-levels-in-dried-herbs" data-anchor="which-regions-report-the-lowest-levels-in-dried-herbs" data-question="Which regions report the lowest levels in dried Herbs?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Which regions report the lowest levels in dried Herbs?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

Among GEMS/Food reporting regions, dried Herbs, as sold had the lowest lead subgroup median in PAHO (60.8 µg/kg) and the highest in SEARO (9,990 µg/kg); reporting regions are markets, not growing areas.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> For cadmium, the lowest regional median was in WPRO (16 µg/kg) and the highest in EURO (470 µg/kg).<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="how-much-of-the-arsenic-in-dried-herbs-is-inorganic" data-anchor="how-much-of-the-arsenic-in-dried-herbs-is-inorganic" data-question="How much of the arsenic in dried Herbs is inorganic?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>How much of the arsenic in dried Herbs is inorganic?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

Inorganic arsenic, the more toxic form, was measured in 7 results from 2 sources, far fewer than total arsenic.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/efsa2014-dietary-exposure-iAs|10]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) · 2014</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/efsa2014-dietary-exposure-iAs">Dietary exposure to inorganic arsenic in the European population</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">EFSA Journal 2014;12(3):3597</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/efsa2014-dietary-exposure-iAs">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) 2014 reported inorganic arsenic at 43.1 µg/kg (mean) in dried Herbs, as sold from European dietary-survey occurrence data.<sup class="cite">[[sources/efsa2014-dietary-exposure-iAs|10]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) · 2014</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/efsa2014-dietary-exposure-iAs">Dietary exposure to inorganic arsenic in the European population</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">EFSA Journal 2014;12(3):3597</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/efsa2014-dietary-exposure-iAs">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>
